title: Om tat sat: the threefold name
hookLine: the three words that hand an act to God
carry: om tat sat: every act offered to god

lines: THREE WORDS TO OFFER AN ACT.
cards: In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and listens. His minister Sanjaya has been granted far sight; he can see the battlefield, and he tells the king every word spoken in Arjuna's chariot.
He's heard Krishna sort food, worship and giving into three kinds. Now, at the very end of chapter seventeen, Krishna gives three words, not for sorting, but for offering. Om.
Tat. Sat. You've met the first one already.
It was your second word, back in camp one.

teach.b: Verse twenty-three. Om tat sat: this is remembered as the threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate. By it, long ago, the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order.
Then Krishna explains each word. Om first. Verse twenty-four: those who follow the Veda always begin their acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline by saying om.
The sound goes first. Tat means that. Verse twenty-five: with tat, people seeking freedom do their sacrifice, discipline and giving without aiming at the reward.
It's a way of saying, this isn't for me; it's for that. And sat means real, true, good. Verse twenty-six: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for any praiseworthy act.
Verse twenty-seven: steadiness in sacrifice, discipline and giving is called sat, and so is any action done for its sake. So the three words make a small arc.
Om: begin with the sacred sound.

teach.h: TAT: FOR THAT, NOT FOR ME.
teach.b: Tat: offer it to that, not to yourself.
Sat: let it be real and good. The chapter's last verse, twenty-eight, ties it back to faith.

teach.h: OM TAT SAT: OFFERED TO GOD.
teach.b: Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called asat, unreal. It counts for nothing, here or after. The Sanskrit prefix a means not, so asat is simply not-sat.
That's the teaching under the three words: in Hinduism, an act can be offered to God, begun with the sacred sound and given away before it's even done.
It's why many Hindus say om before a prayer or a reading, and why some close a reading or a puja with om tat sat, handing it back.

how: Some Hindus say 'om tat sat' at the close of a reading, a ritual or a teaching; some printed Gitas set the three words in each chapter's closing line, and verse 17.24 says Vedic rites begin with om.

o: a seated posture held during meditation
the last verse that closes a temple chant
what is real and true, and also good

games.q: the threefold name — tap the pairs.
p: done without faith: counts for nothing

s: om tat sat is called the threefold name of Brahman in Gita 17.23
by it the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order.
sat means only 'existence' and has nothing to do with goodness
verse 26: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for praiseworthy acts.
the Gita says acts done without faith still count fully
verse 28: they're called asat, and count for nothing, here or after.

games.q: you're about to begin an act of giving and you want it to be for that, not for you. which word does verse 25 attach to this?
games.why: tat, that. seekers of freedom act with tat, without aiming at the reward.

practice: Think of one ordinary thing you'll do after this: cooking, a call, a task at work. If you pray, offer it the way the verses do: say om softly, the beginning; then tat, this is for you, not for me; then sat, may it be real and good.
If you don't pray, take three breaths with those three thoughts. Then just sit, and let the action wait.

wordCard.voice: Sat, the real, the good. Gita seventeen, twenty-three: the threefold name of the ultimate, om tat sat; om is the sacred sound, tat is that, and sat is the real and good.

orig.note: Sanskrit: om (the sacred syllable), tat (that), sat (the real, the good); the threefold name in Gita 17.23.

carryVoice: Your line: om tat sat, every act offered to God. Begin with om, give it to that, let it be sat. Tomorrow, the Gita's last chapter.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 17.23 (the threefold name of Brahman)
